title: ZPPO: Put the Teacher in the Prompt, Not the Gradient
hook: A small student learns from a bigger teacher without the drift that breaks on-policy RL - by feeding the teacher's answer into the prompt as a candidate to judge, never into the gradient.
key_points: Problem: distilling logits into a small student over-fits the teacher's sharpest modes; injecting teacher answers into the RL gradient breaks the on-policy assumption and causes drift.
ZPPO keeps the teacher inside the prompt, not the policy gradient — inspired by Vygotsky's 'zone of proximal development.'

On hard questions it builds two prompts: a Binary Candidate question (discriminate the correct teacher answer from the student's wrong one) and a Negative Candidate question (pool failed rollouts to expose shared mistakes).
A prompt replay buffer recirculates each hard question until the student's mean rollout accuracy reaches half, then graduates it.
Across 0.8B-9B students with a 27B teacher on 31 benchmarks, it beats off/on-policy distillation and GRPO — with the largest gains at the smallest scale.
content_html: Knowledge distillation is brittle for small students: forcing a tiny model to imitate a big teacher's logits concentrates it on the teacher's sharpest modes and hurts generalization. Reinforcement learning sidesteps logit imitation by training on the student's own rollouts — but on questions where every rollout fails, the advantage is zero and the data is discarded. Splicing a stronger teacher's answer into the policy gradient to rescue those cases breaks the on-policy assumption and induces drift.
extra_html: Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization (ZPPO), from an NVIDIA-led team, resolves this by keeping the teacher in the prompt rather than the gradient — borrowing Vygotsky's "zone of proximal development." For hard questions it constructs two reformulated prompts: a Binary Candidate-included Question pairs a correct teacher response with an incorrect student one as anonymized candidates to discriminate, and a Negative Candidate-included Question aggregates the student's wrong rollouts to surface their shared failure modes. A replay buffer keeps recirculating each hard question until the student's mean accuracy reaches half. Tested on the Qwen3.5 family at four scales (0.8B–9B) with a 27B teacher across 31 benchmarks, the authors report it outperforms off- and on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the biggest gains at the smallest scale.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

related.title: On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation
related.hook: On-policy distillation isn't a midpoint between fine-tuning and RL — it carves its own narrow path through parameter space, locking into a low-dimensional subspace early in training.

related.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
related.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

flashcards.prompt: What is ZPPO's core idea versus standard distillation and RL?
flashcards.back_html: Keep the teacher in the prompt — as candidate answers the student must judge — rather than in the policy gradient. This avoids both logit over-imitation (distillation) and the on-policy drift caused by injecting teacher answers into the gradient.

flashcards.prompt: On hard questions, what do ZPPO's BCQ and NCQ prompts do?

choices.text: BCQ makes the student discriminate a correct teacher answer from its own wrong one; NCQ pools its failed rollouts to surface shared mistakes
They distill the teacher's output logits directly into the student
They add extra parameters and experts to the student model

flashcards.explanation_html: BCQ (Binary Candidate-included Question) and NCQ (Negative Candidate-included Question) reformulate the prompt so the teacher's signal arrives as candidates to reason over, keeping training on-policy.

flashcards.prompt: Where does ZPPO's name come from, and what does its replay buffer do?
flashcards.back_html: From Vygotsky's "zone of proximal development." A prompt replay buffer recirculates each hard question until the student's mean rollout accuracy reaches half, then graduates it (or FIFO-evicts it under finite capacity).
